doctrine.title: Power Is Task-Specific
doctrine.statement: Interpret power within the movement, load, body mass, force-time constraints, and measurement method used to express it.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Established / Known. Mechanical power may be expressed as work over time and, in aligned conditions, as force × velocity — but neither relationship establishes that a high power measurement represents a stable trait independent of task, body mass, equipment, calculation method, and movement strategy. [EP105-01, EP105-02, EP105-08]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: This does not make power measurement useless. It makes an unlabeled power number meaningless. Every power value in G3 carries its task, load, and calculation method.

doctrine.title: Related Qualities Are Not Interchangeable
doctrine.statement: Strength, force, impulse, velocity, power, and RFD interact but are distinct.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Established / Known for the mechanical distinctions; A for definition, B/C for routine field interpretation in the case of RFD. [EP105-01, EP105-02, EP105-03]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Distinct does not mean unrelated — these qualities interact continuously in every athletic task. The doctrine forbids substitution, not integration. "Explosiveness" is Class F as a precise diagnostic term and is replaced by the actual quality and task.

doctrine.title: Power Development Is Method-Neutral
doctrine.statement: Plyometrics, ballistic resistance exercise, sprinting, resistance training, medicine-ball work, and weightlifting derivatives can all contribute. No method is universally required.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported Practice that multiple method families are effective for power-related outcomes when selected for the athlete, task, and context; F for any claim that a named method is universally superior or universally required. The Evidence Pack rates the comparative method evidence B, never A, and G3 does not raise it. Plyometric-versus-resistance comparisons show no consistent difference for jump outcomes, with mixed sprint findings; weightlifting and plyometric training may yield similar improvements in several outcomes. [EP105-02, EP105-04, EP105-14, EP105-15]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Method-neutral is not method-indifferent. Methods differ in learning cost, equipment demand, fatigue cost, and coachability — which is exactly what AS-105-03 asks the coach to weigh. No G3 material may require any exercise or method.

doctrine.title: Strength Supports Power but Does Not Gate It
doctrine.statement: Strength matters, especially in weaker and less-trained athletes, but G3 does not require a universal strength phase or squat ratio before appropriate power training.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Known that strength is a contributor to power; B — Probable that weaker athletes often benefit materially from strength development; F for the claim that athletes must get strong before any power training, and F for a universal squat-ratio prerequisite — a youth resistance-training review specifically states that the frequently proposed 1.5×-bodyweight squat prerequisite for lower-body plyometrics is not supported. [EP105-02, EP105-10, EP105-11]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Rejecting the gate is not rejecting strength. Competence, exposure, readiness, supervision, and task demand still govern what an athlete does (AS-105-06) — those are coaching judgments, not a ratio.

doctrine.title: Acute Output Does Not Dictate Chronic Prescription
doctrine.statement: The load producing the highest acute measured power is not automatically the best long-term training load.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Established as a distinction. Maximal measured power often occurs at an intermediate load, but the exact load varies by exercise, athlete, measurement method, external versus system power, body mass, and peak versus mean outcome; training outcomes depend on stimulus, specificity, volume, technical quality, fatigue, athlete status, and concurrent training. The universal "30% 1RM" rule is F. [EP105-02, EP105-08]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: No load percentage is published anywhere in this course (CJ-01, CJ-02). Acute peak-power testing may describe an exercise response for an athlete; it does not set the chronic training load.

doctrine.title: Output Quality Governs Power Training
doctrine.statement: Preserve movement intent, technical execution, and output quality appropriate to the objective. Fatigue that materially changes the task changes the stimulus.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported Practice. Power work generally requires more recovery than hypertrophy-oriented training when the priority is preserving velocity, jump height, technical execution, or output; exact rest requirements vary by task, load, athlete, and objective. [EP105-02]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: No rest interval, repetition count, or velocity-loss cutoff is published (CJ-10, CJ-11). "Fatigue makes power work more sport-specific" is an F/B boundary claim: training under fatigue may develop fatigue tolerance, but it does not make maximal-power work more specific.

doctrine.title: Transfer Must Be Demonstrated, Not Assumed
doctrine.statement: Improvement in a jump, lift, throw, profile, or laboratory metric does not automatically establish sport transfer.
doctrine.evidence_note: A — Established. Power-related test outcomes are commonly associated with sprinting, jumping, and COD, but association does not identify the causal quality to train; isolated improvements in a training exercise cannot be assumed to transfer to sport performance. [EP105-02, EP105-07, EP105-14, EP105-15]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Continuous with G3 103 D103-7 and G3 104 D104-2. This is not a claim that transfer is rare — it is a requirement that the transfer pathway be stated and, where possible, observed.

doctrine.title: Directional Similarity Is Not Sufficient Specificity
doctrine.statement: Horizontal, vertical, unilateral, bilateral, or visually sport-like exercises do not guarantee direction- or sport-specific transfer.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported Practice for considering direction and task demands; F for automatic vector-matching claims and for the blanket claim that unilateral work is inherently more sport-specific. [EP105-02, EP105-07, EP105-13]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Direction may matter. What is unsupported is the inference from visual direction to guaranteed transfer. Selecting unilateral or bilateral work by task, competence, tolerance, and desired loading is Class D — legitimate coaching inference, labeled as such (CJ-12).

doctrine.title: Profiling Generates Hypotheses
doctrine.statement: Force–velocity profiles may describe performance and support hypotheses; profile labels are not definitive diagnoses.
doctrine.evidence_class: B for describing performance across selected loads with transparent protocol; C/D for generating training hypotheses; F for definitively diagnosing "force deficiency" or "velocity deficiency," for using an "optimal profile" as an exact target for all athletes, and for replacing sprint/jump testing, technical observation, and sport context
doctrine.evidence_note: B for describing performance across selected loads with transparent protocol; C/D for generating training hypotheses; F for definitively diagnosing "force deficiency" or "velocity deficiency," for using an "optimal profile" as an exact target for all athletes, and for replacing sprint/jump testing, technical observation, and sport context. Reliability is method-dependent — reported slope reliability across methods has been poor, and validity differs by method. Recent meta-analytic evidence on profile-based individualized training is C — Emerging. [EP105-05, EP105-06, EP105-07, EP105-16, EP105-25]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: The model–measurement rule (§2.4) governs this doctrine. A profile is a description produced by assumptions. No F-V threshold, deficit classification, or optimal-profile target is published (CJ-03, CJ-04).

doctrine.title: Technology Must Serve a Decision
doctrine.statement: Force plates, VBT, jump apps, and profiling systems are useful only when sufficiently reliable, interpretable, and actionable.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported Practice. VBT usefulness depends on device validity, exercise specificity, loading, familiarity, and whether the measure changes a coaching decision; force plates improve data availability, not necessarily decision quality; app and device validation is not automatically transferable across software, protocols, or users. "VBT is required" is F. [EP105-08, EP105-17, EP105-24]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Low-tech environments must remain capable of G3-quality coaching. The course is written so that a coach with a tape measure and a stopwatch loses no conceptual ground.

doctrine.title: Simple Reliable Metrics Outrank Metric Volume
doctrine.statement: Prioritize standardized, reliable, decision-relevant measures over dashboard complexity.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported Practice. CMJ metric reviews report stronger reliability for several basic outcome metrics and less consistent reliability for selected RFD, eccentric, stiffness, and derived variables. More metrics can create more noise. [EP105-08, EP105-09]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: This is not an argument against force plates. It is an argument for a small, pre-specified, reliable metric set chosen before the data is collected.

doctrine.title: Reactive Metrics Are Task Measures
doctrine.statement: RSI, RSI-modified, jump height, contact time, and force-plate variables do not independently define readiness, stiffness, injury risk, or explosiveness.
doctrine.evidence_class: A that RSI is a standardized task-specific ratio; F for the claim that RSI alone completely measures reactive ability; F/C for the claim that low RSI directly identifies a tendon-stiffness deficit; B/C for RSI and RSI-modified contributing to a broader standardized monitoring battery
doctrine.evidence_note: A that RSI is a standardized task-specific ratio; F for the claim that RSI alone completely measures reactive ability; F/C for the claim that low RSI directly identifies a tendon-stiffness deficit; B/C for RSI and RSI-modified contributing to a broader standardized monitoring battery. [EP105-08, EP105-24]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: These metrics are worth collecting when standardized and decision-relevant. They are not worth a label.

doctrine.title: Acute Potentiation Is Not Chronic Superiority
doctrine.statement: PAPE may be useful conditionally; it does not establish long-term superiority of complex or contrast methods.
doctrine.evidence_class: B/C for acute conditional PAPE effects, which are small and variable and context-dependent; C/B for chronic complex and contrast training, where superiority over simpler programming is not consistently established; F for "PAPE proves complex training is superior
doctrine.evidence_note: B/C for acute conditional PAPE effects, which are small and variable and context-dependent; C/B for chronic complex and contrast training, where superiority over simpler programming is not consistently established; F for "PAPE proves complex training is superior." PAP and PAPE are not interchangeable terms. [EP105-17, EP105-18]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Where the Evidence Pack reports an acute response window from a specific analyzed study set, that figure describes those studies. It is not a G3 prescription and is never published as one (CJ-05).

doctrine.title: Youth Can Train Power
doctrine.statement: Properly supervised and progressively exposed youth can sprint, jump, land, throw, perform plyometrics, and use appropriate ballistic and resistance methods without arbitrary age or strength-ratio gates.
doctrine.evidence_note: A/B — Established/Supported. Youth resistance and plyometric training can improve strength, jump, sprint, and other fitness outcomes when appropriately supervised and progressed; evidence does not support age-based prohibitions or arbitrary strength thresholds as universal gates. "Youth must wait until age 16," "youth need a universal strength threshold before jumping," and "youth should not do plyometrics" are all F. [EP105-10, EP105-11, EP105-12, EP105-13]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: The claim is conditioned on supervision, technical coaching, and progression — stated every time (AS-105-14). And youth evidence does not validate adult loading, volume, or testing prescriptions for middle-school athletes (Condition 2).

doctrine.title: Power Programming Is Integrated Load Management
doctrine.statement: Coordinate power exposure with sprinting, jumping, strength, practice, competition, and recovery. No universal contact count, frequency, microcycle, or maintenance dose governs all athletes.
doctrine.evidence_note: B — Supported Practice for integrating power exposure with total high-intensity load; D for exact microcycle templates; U — Unknown for exact in-season maintenance and minimum-effective doses; F for universal contact classifications. [EP105-02, EP105-19, EP105-21]
doctrine.teaching_boundary: Continuous with G3 103 D103-8 and G3 104 D104-12. The athlete's jumps in practice count. No frequency, contact count, or maintenance dose is published (CJ-08, CJ-13, CJ-15).

applied_standards.title: Name the Output
applied_standards.statement: Identify the actual task and output requirement before prescribing "power."
applied_standards.enforcement: every power_task object requires output_requirement and task (§21.4).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Build Limitation Hypotheses From Multiple Sources
applied_standards.statement: Use task performance, strength/force capacity, technical observation, training history, and context before labeling an athlete.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: B — the Evidence Pack's own supported-practice position.
applied_standards.boundary: the output is a provisional hypothesis, not an identity (D105-09, CJ-04).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Use the Simplest Effective Method
applied_standards.statement: Where multiple methods can meet the objective, prefer the best benefit-to-cost option for athlete, coach, facility, and calendar.
applied_standards.boundary: "simplest" means lowest total cost to deliver well, not lowest effort.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Preserve Intended Quality
applied_standards.statement: Manage reps, sets, rest, and exercise selection so output and technique remain consistent with the intended adaptation.
applied_standards.boundary: no rest interval, repetition count, or velocity-loss cutoff is published (CJ-10, CJ-11).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Progress Plyometric Demand, Not Just Contacts
applied_standards.statement: Progress landing demand, velocity, amplitude, direction, unilateral demand, external load, complexity, and exposure.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: B for progressive individualized dosage; F for universal contact classifications as evidence-based prescriptions.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: No Universal Strength Gate
applied_standards.statement: Use competence, exposure, readiness, supervision, and task demands instead of arbitrary bodyweight ratios.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Separate Acute and Chronic Evidence
applied_standards.statement: Do not use PAPE, acute peak-power loads, or acute force-plate responses as proof of superior long-term programming.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: A as a methodological rule (D105-05, D105-13).
applied_standards.enforcement: acute and chronic claims are cited and labeled separately in every module evidence block.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Treat F-V Labels as Provisional
applied_standards.statement: Force- and velocity-deficit labels require corroboration.
applied_standards.enforcement: NovaKore stores a limitation hypothesis with confidence and review point; no label may be stored as a fixed athlete attribute.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Standardize Testing
applied_standards.statement: Define protocol, equipment, warm-up, instructions, calculation method, and baseline.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: A/B — reliability depends on task standardization, device, familiarization, and calculation. Inherited: G3 102 AS-06 (conditions recorded at time of testing).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Measure the Construct Actually Tested
applied_standards.statement: Label CMJ, broad jump, RSI, loaded jump, medicine-ball throw, or bar-velocity results according to the task performed.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Use Technology Only When Actionable
applied_standards.statement: Technology must answer a defined question.
applied_standards.boundary: the question is defined before the data is collected; a metric that changes no decision is not collected.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Interpret Change Against Error and Baseline
applied_standards.statement: Readiness and performance changes require repeated baselines, reliability and error context, and other athlete information.
applied_standards.evidence_basis: B/C for multi-source monitoring; F for single-metric automated readiness decisions.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: No Universal Asymmetry Threshold
applied_standards.statement: A fixed 10% or 15% value does not automatically trigger intervention.
applied_standards.standing: binding prohibition. G3 publishes no threshold and substitutes none (CJ-20).
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Youth Progress by Competence and Exposure
applied_standards.statement: Supervise, progressively dose, technically coach, and scale to maturity and training age without unsupported prohibitions.
applied_standards.enforcement: supervision ratio documented for every G3 youth power group; the safety claim is stated with its conditions.
applied_standards.label: applied_standard

applied_standards.title: Integrate the Weekly High-Output Load
applied_standards.statement: Account for total sprint, jump, COD, strength, practice, and competition exposure.
applied_standards.boundary: no frequency, contact count, microcycle model, or maintenance dose is published (CJ-08, CJ-13, CJ-14, CJ-15, CJ-16).

claim_audit.claim: Build strength before training any power
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Concurrent and progressive development is feasible. Strength contributes, especially in weaker athletes; it does not gate power exposure. D105-04, AS-105-06. [EP105-11, EP105-10]

claim_audit.claim: A 1.5× or 2× bodyweight squat is required before plyometrics
claim_audit.g3_teaches: No universal validated threshold exists; a youth resistance-training review states the proposed prerequisite is unsupported. Progress by competence, exposure, and supervision. D105-04, AS-105-06, AS-105-14. [EP105-10]

claim_audit.claim: Power training must use light loads
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Effective power methods span loading conditions. Load is chosen for the adaptation intended, not for a category. D105-03, D105-06. [EP105-02]

claim_audit.claim: 30% of 1RM is the universally optimal power load
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Load–power relationships are exercise-, athlete-, and metric-specific. No percentage is prescribed as universal. D105-05, CJ-01, CJ-02. [EP105-02]

claim_audit.claim: The load that maximizes acute peak power is the best chronic training load
claim_audit.g3_teaches: An acute peak-power test describes an exercise response. It does not determine the training load that produces the best adaptation. This is the single most common technically-literate error in power programming. D105-05, AS-105-07. [EP105-02]

claim_audit.claim: Olympic lifts are required for athletes — or are inherently too dangerous for them
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Weightlifting derivatives are one viable, effective method family. They are not mandatory, and they are not dangerous independent of supervision, progression, competence, and context. Both absolutes fail; they fail in opposite directions. D105-03, AS-105-03. [EP105-04, EP105-10]

claim_audit.claim: Catching is necessary for power development
claim_audit.g3_teaches: No-catch derivatives may retain meaningful force-velocity exposure while reducing receiving-position constraints; direct comparative evidence is limited. Catch or no-catch is a benefit-to-cost decision, and the comparison is C. D105-03, CJ-07.

claim_audit.claim: Plyometrics are inherently high risk
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Risk depends on programming, progression, surface, fatigue, competence, and supervision. Poorly managed exposure can be risky; supervised progression is supported. The blanket claim is unsupported in either direction. D105-03, §19. [EP105-10]

claim_audit.claim: Youth should not perform plyometrics
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Supervised, progressive jumping, landing, and plyometric work is supported in youth populations. Age is not the gate; competence, exposure, maturation, and supervision are. D105-14, AS-105-14. [EP105-13, EP105-10]

claim_audit.claim: Depth jumps are the best plyometric
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Task- and athlete-dependent; no universal superiority. Depth jumps are a high-demand exercise with real prerequisites, not a default. D105-03, AS-105-05. [EP105-02]

claim_audit.claim: More contacts produce more power
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Plyometric dose-response evidence is heterogeneous and does not support universal contact classifications. Progress the demand — height, intensity, complexity, direction, and quality — not the count. AS-105-05, CJ-08. [EP105-19, EP105-21]

claim_audit.claim: Every jump should be maximal
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Purpose, fatigue state, learning demand, and landing requirement differ across tasks. Some plyometric work is deliberately submaximal. D105-06, AS-105-04. [EP105-02]

claim_audit.claim: Jump training automatically improves sprinting
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Jump training often improves sprint outcomes, but transfer is conditional on task, athlete, and program context — and improvement in the exercise is not itself transfer. D105-07, AS-105-01. [EP105-14, EP105-15]

claim_audit.claim: Directional similarity guarantees transfer — horizontal jumps to acceleration, vertical jumps to maximum velocity
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Directional similarity is not sufficient specificity. Force-time characteristics, coordination, and task constraints all differ. Vector-matching is a hypothesis, not a mechanism. D105-08. [EP105-02, EP105-06]

claim_audit.claim: Unilateral work is inherently more sport-specific
claim_audit.g3_teaches: No inherent superiority is established. Unilateral and bilateral work each have a place; the choice reflects the task, the athlete, and what is being developed. D105-08, D105-03. [EP105-02]

claim_audit.claim: Strength and power must be trained in separate phases
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Concurrent and mixed approaches are defensible. Phase separation is an organizational choice, not a physiological requirement. D105-04, §17.4. [EP105-02, EP105-11]

claim_audit.claim: Explosive intent matters only with light loads
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Intent to move the load rapidly is relevant across the loading spectrum, including heavy loads. Intent is coached, not assumed. D105-06, AS-105-04. [EP105-02]

claim_audit.claim: VBT is required for power training
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Velocity-based training is an optional measurement and prescription tool that is device-, exercise-, and load-specific. It is not required, and a G3 coach without it is not disadvantaged in decision quality. D105-10, AS-105-11, §15.5. [EP105-17]

claim_audit.claim: Force plates reveal exactly why a jump was poor
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Force plates measure force over time. They show what happened, not why. Many derived metrics are model-based and reliability-limited. D105-10, D105-11, §15.4. [EP105-08, EP105-09]

claim_audit.claim: RSI completely measures reactive ability
claim_audit.g3_teaches: RSI is a task-specific ratio of flight time to contact time under one protocol. It is not a measure of reactive ability in general, of tendon stiffness, or of injury risk. D105-12. [EP105-08]

claim_audit.claim: Interlimb asymmetry above 10% is automatically a problem
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Asymmetry is task-, direction-, and reliability-dependent. No universal 10% or 15% cutoff is established as automatically performance-limiting, injury-predictive, or corrective. Repeated, task-specific, reliable monitoring is B/C; the universal cutoff is F. AS-105-13. [EP105-08]

claim_audit.claim: CMJ height alone measures readiness
claim_audit.g3_teaches: CMJ height is a standardized jump outcome. Readiness inference requires multi-source context — protocol, baseline, typical error, athlete-reported state, training load, and sport context. Multi-source monitoring is B/C; the single-metric decision is F. D105-11, AS-105-11. [EP105-08]

claim_audit.claim: PAPE proves complex training is superior
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Acute post-activation performance enhancement can occur in selected athletes and protocols. An acute response does not establish chronic programming superiority. D105-13, AS-105-07. [EP105-17]

claim_audit.claim: Cluster sets are inherently better for power
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Cluster configurations are potentially useful under a quality-preservation rationale, and that rationale is coherent. Inherent superiority is not established. The method is an organizational choice, not an upgrade. D105-13, D105-06. [EP105-18]

claim_audit.claim: Soreness proves plyometric effectiveness
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Soreness is not an adaptation marker and not an outcome measure. It is information about exposure and tolerance. §19.

claim_audit.claim: Fatigue makes power work more sport-specific
claim_audit.g3_teaches: Training under fatigue may develop fatigue tolerance — a legitimate objective, deliberately programmed. It does not develop maximal power output, and calling it sport-specific conceals the substitution. D105-06, AS-105-04.

claim_audit_symmetry_rule: Every correction is a correction, not an inversion. Inverting an audited claim fails competency C105-18 from the other side and is scored as a failure.

modules.title: What Power Actually Is
modules.framing_statement: "He needs to be more explosive" is not a coaching statement. It names no task, no quality, and no decision — and this course begins by taking it away.
modules.purpose: To install the mechanical vocabulary the course depends on, and to end the use of "explosiveness" as a diagnostic category.

learning_objectives.objective: Define mechanical power as rate of work, and state when force × velocity applies.
Distinguish force, strength, work, power, impulse, RFD, velocity, and acceleration.
Distinguish peak and mean power, and state why interval and calculation must be specified.
Explain why relative power is not universally more meaningful than absolute power.
Explain why "explosiveness" is not a stable scientific construct.
Replace an "explosiveness" statement with the actual quality and task.

evidence_classifications.statement: Force, strength, work, mechanical power, impulse, velocity, and acceleration are distinct constructs
Mechanical power is rate of work; force × velocity applies when vectors are aligned
Peak power is the highest instantaneous power in a defined interval and model
Mean power requires its interval and calculation to be specified
RFD is distinct from power
evidence_classifications.class: A for definition; B/C for routine field interpretation

evidence_classifications.statement: Relative power is context dependent, not universally superior
"Explosiveness" as a precise diagnostic term

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: definitional evidence is mechanical and not population-limited; the field-interpretation caveat on RFD carries adult laboratory origins.
modules.coach_judgment: none. Definitions are not negotiable inside G3.

lessons.title: The word that means nothing
lessons.content: Four coaches use "explosive" for four different qualities in one session. The cost is that none of them can select a method or a test.

lessons.title: Power, properly defined
lessons.content: Rate of work; force × velocity in aligned conditions; and why the definition already contains the task-specificity of D105-01.

lessons.title: The neighbours
lessons.content: Force, strength, work, impulse, velocity, acceleration — each defined against power and against each other.

lessons.title: Peak, mean, and the protocol
lessons.content: Why a power number without its interval, model, and device is not a result.

lessons.title: Relative and absolute
lessons.content: When normalizing helps, when it distorts, and why neither is universally superior.

lessons.title: RFD, introduced honestly
lessons.content: Conceptually important, measurement-sensitive, and not a synonym for power. Full treatment in M8.

lessons.title: Rewriting the claim
lessons.content: Coaches convert real statements — "she needs more explosiveness," "he's a power athlete" — into task-and-quality language, or flag them as unanswerable.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied immediately to G3 session plans and testing language. A block labeled "power" is incomplete; "vertical projection output in a loaded jump for an athlete whose demand is repeated jump performance" can be evaluated by someone else.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Using "explosiveness" as a diagnosis (D105-02; Class F as a precise term) · reporting a power value with no task or calculation · using power and RFD interchangeably · assuming relative power is always the better expression · treating a peak-power figure as an athlete attribute.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M1-A — Rewrite the claim. Eight real coaching statements rewritten into G3 form with task, quality, and measurement named — or flagged as unanswerable without more information.

knowledge_assessment.item: Which definition of mechanical power does G3 use?
Match seven constructs to their defining relationship.
A peak-power value reported without its protocol is best described as…
"Relative power is the more meaningful measure for athletes."
Rewrite "he needs to be more explosive" in G3 terms.

applied_assessment.title: Power language audit
applied_assessment.description: A real program or testing document annotated so every power claim names task, quality, and measurement, with unanswerable claims flagged.
applied_assessment.standard: every claim rewritten or flagged; no "explosiveness" as a diagnosis; no collapsing of power, RFD, and impulse.

modules.practical_sign_off_linkage: None. Terminology accuracy carries into PS-1 and is scored in T-01.

modules.title: Mechanical Foundations & Athletic Transfer
modules.framing_statement: Jump height can improve for at least five different reasons. Until you know which one, you do not know what you trained.
modules.purpose: To ground power reasoning in impulse, force-time, and body mass, and to install the association-versus-transfer discipline before any method is discussed.

learning_objectives.objective: Explain work/time and force × velocity as descriptions, not prescriptions.
Explain impulse–momentum and why net impulse relative to body mass governs takeoff velocity.
Name the multiple pathways by which a jump outcome can change.
Explain force-time constraints — why time available changes which quality matters.
Distinguish association from transfer.
Explain why directional similarity does not guarantee transfer.
State a transfer pathway for any method proposed.

evidence_classifications.statement: Force and velocity jointly determine external mechanical power
Impulse is the force-time integral; net vertical impulse relative to body mass determines takeoff velocity
Jump height can change through force magnitude, force-application time, timing/coordination, movement strategy, or body mass
Impulse is often more task-informative than peak force alone when time is constrained
evidence_classifications.class: A/B — mechanical principle; task application is reasonable extrapolation

evidence_classifications.statement: Power-related test outcomes are associated with sprinting, jumping, and COD
Association does not identify the causal quality to train
Resistance training can improve sport-specific performance in elite athletes
evidence_classifications.class: B — spans different sports and interventions
evidence_classifications.basis: Evidence Pack §5; supporting record not itemized (§20.3b)

evidence_classifications.statement: Directional similarity guarantees transfer
Vertical jump alone predicts or develops maximal velocity

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: transfer evidence spans athlete populations with substantial heterogeneity; elite-sample findings are not generalized to developing athletes.
modules.coach_judgment: which pathway to pursue for a given athlete — that is M3's hypothesis work.

lessons.title: Work, time, force, velocity
lessons.content: The mechanics, stated so they describe rather than prescribe.

lessons.title: Impulse and momentum
lessons.content: The force-time integral, and why it is the honest way to think about jumping and acceleration.

lessons.title: Five ways a jump improves
lessons.content: Force magnitude · force-application time · timing and coordination · movement strategy · body mass. This lesson is the mechanical basis for the entire limitation-hypothesis method in M3.

lessons.title: Time available changes the question
lessons.content: When time is constrained, peak force achieved too late does not help — which is why impulse and RFD enter the conversation, and why neither is universally primary.

lessons.title: Association is not transfer
lessons.content: Test outcomes correlate with sport tasks. That identifies neither the limiting quality nor the method.

lessons.title: Direction, carefully
lessons.content: Horizontal and vertical tasks can both contribute to sprint-related outcomes; visual direction alone establishes nothing (D105-08).

lessons.title: Stating the transfer pathway
lessons.content: For any method: what adaptation, expressed in which task, supported by what exposure, and what would show it did not occur.

modules.coaching_applications: The practical use is diagnostic restraint. When an athlete's jump improves, the competent coach can name which pathways plausibly moved and which were not addressed — before deciding what the improvement means.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Treating jump height as a power diagnosis · reading a correlation as a prescription · vector-matching claims (CA-14) · assuming vertical work develops maximal velocity · ignoring body mass in tasks the athlete must move · reporting exercise improvement as sport transfer (§1.2).

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M2-A — The improved jump. An athlete's CMJ rises 3 cm across a block that included strength work, plyometrics, and a body-mass change. The learner lists the plausible pathways, states what can and cannot be concluded, and says what would distinguish them.

knowledge_assessment.item: Which pathways can change jump height?
Net vertical impulse relative to body mass primarily determines…
A study reports r = 0.65 between CMJ and sprint time. What follows for programming?
"We do horizontal jumps because acceleration is horizontal." Identify the error.
State a transfer pathway for a method you currently use.

applied_assessment.title: Transfer statement
applied_assessment.description: For one athlete and one method: demand, output requirement, intended adaptation, transfer pathway, supporting exposure, and the falsifier.
applied_assessment.standard: association and transfer distinguished; no vector-matching claim; body mass considered where relevant; falsifier stated in task terms.

modules.prerequisite_gating:
Prerequisite: M1 at standard. Unlocks: M3. Gate: none.

modules.title: Strength–Power Relationship & Athlete Limitation Hypotheses
modules.framing_statement: "Force-limited" is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis, and not an identity. The skill is holding it loosely enough to be wrong.
modules.purpose: To establish what strength contributes to power and where that contribution ends, and to teach the multi-source, provisional limitation hypothesis that drives every method decision in this course.

learning_objectives.objective: State what maximal strength contributes to power output.
Explain why the contribution is generally larger in weaker or less-trained athletes.
Explain diminishing returns and task-specific limits.
Reject the universal strength-before-power sequence and the universal squat ratio.
Build a limitation hypothesis from multiple sources.
State the confidence level and review point for any hypothesis.
Revise or abandon a hypothesis the response does not support.

evidence_classifications.statement: Strength is a contributor to power
evidence_classifications.class: A / Known — contribution differs with task and athlete status

evidence_classifications.statement: Weaker or less-trained athletes often benefit materially from strength development
evidence_classifications.class: B / Probable — "weak" must be task- and population-contextualized

evidence_classifications.statement: Concurrent development of strength and power-oriented tasks is supported in many populations
Athletes must get strong before any power training
A universal squat ratio is required before plyometrics
evidence_classifications.class: F — no validated universal threshold; the 1.5× prerequisite is explicitly unsupported

evidence_classifications.statement: More strength always produces more sport power
evidence_classifications.class: F — diminishing returns and task-specific limits exist

evidence_classifications.statement: Strength and power require separate phases
evidence_classifications.class: F — concurrent and mixed approaches are defensible

evidence_classifications.statement: A single metric identifies the limiting quality

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: the strength–power evidence is adult-weighted; the squat-ratio rejection derives from a youth-focused review and is stated with that origin.
modules.coach_judgment: the hypothesis itself, its confidence, and its review point (CJ-05, CJ-06).

lessons.title: What strength buys
lessons.content: Larger force capacity can increase force available across velocities. Real, and neither complete nor independent of coordination and velocity expression.

lessons.title: Who benefits most
lessons.content: The contribution is generally more consequential in weaker or less-trained athletes — which makes "weak" a contextual judgment, not a number.

lessons.title: Where it stops
lessons.content: Diminishing returns; task-specific limits; and why "more strength always means more power" is Class F.

lessons.title: No gate
lessons.content: The universal strength phase and the squat-ratio prerequisite are unsupported, the latter explicitly. What replaces them: competence, exposure, readiness, supervision, and task demand (AS-105-06).

lessons.title: Building the hypothesis
lessons.content: Five sources: task performance, force capacity, technical observation, training history, and context. A hypothesis built on one of them is a label.

lessons.title: Confidence and review
lessons.content: Every hypothesis carries how confident the coach is and when it will be revisited. This is what makes it provisional rather than an identity (AS-105-08).

lessons.title: Being wrong well
lessons.content: What a non-response means, and how to abandon a hypothesis without abandoning the athlete's block.

modules.coaching_applications: Applied at every G3 intake and every phase review. The artifact is a two-sentence hypothesis with its sources, confidence, and review point — short enough that coaches actually write it.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Strength-before-power absolutes (CA-01) · squat-ratio prerequisites (CA-02) · separate-phase requirements (CA-16) · labels treated as identities · single-source hypotheses · never revisiting a hypothesis that the response contradicted.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M3-A — Strong and slow. A strong high-school athlete with poor acceleration. The learner builds the hypothesis from all five sources and states what would refute it. Developed in full as Case 2 (§10.2).

knowledge_assessment.item: The strength–power relationship is best described as…
Which sources contribute to a G3 limitation hypothesis?
"He needs a 1.5× squat before we start plyos." Identify the errors.
A limitation hypothesis differs from a diagnosis because…
State what would make you abandon your current hypothesis for one athlete.

applied_assessment.title: Limitation hypothesis
applied_assessment.description: For one athlete: the output requirement, the five sources, the provisional hypothesis, the confidence level, the review point, and the falsifier.
applied_assessment.standard: multi-source; provisional language throughout; no gate or ratio; falsifier stated.

modules.practical_sign_off_linkage: PS-1 (completed at M4). Observed elements from M3: the coach states a hypothesis and its confidence out loud, from real athlete information.

Prerequisite: M2 at standard. Unlocks: M4. Gate: none.

modules.title: Force–Velocity & Load–Power Models
modules.framing_statement: A profile is a description produced by assumptions. It can start a conversation. It cannot end one.
modules.purpose: To teach F-V profiling and load-power relationships accurately — what they describe, what they cannot diagnose, and why the load that maximizes acute power is not automatically the training load.

learning_objectives.objective: Describe F0, V0, Pmax, slope, imbalance, and "optimal profile" as modeled outputs.
State the reliability and validity limits of vertical-jump profiling methods.
Explain why external load-velocity relationships are not the intrinsic muscle force-velocity relationship.
Describe the load-power curve and why the peak load varies.
Distinguish acute peak-power load from optimal chronic training load.
Use a profile to generate a hypothesis without diagnostic overreach.
State when profiling should be optional, advanced, or excluded.

evidence_classifications.statement: F-V models combine measured variables with modeled theoretical outputs and are not direct measurements of muscular capacity
Vertical-jump profiles can show high linearity while slope reliability across methods is poor
evidence_classifications.class: B — reported coefficients of variation of 14–30% in the cited reliability work

evidence_classifications.statement: Validity is method-dependent; one common method showed poor-to-fair validity while a two-point method with distal loads performed better
Describing performance across selected loads with transparent protocol
Generating training hypotheses from a profile
evidence_classifications.class: C/D — when corroborated by performance and observation

evidence_classifications.statement: Definitively diagnosing "force deficiency" or "velocity deficiency"
Using "optimal profile" as an exact target for all athletes
Replacing sprint/jump testing, technical observation, and sport context with profiling
Profile-based individualized training improving vertical-profile outcomes and jump height
evidence_classifications.class: C — Emerging; sprint effects non-significant in one review

evidence_classifications.statement: Maximal measured power often occurs at an intermediate load
The exact peak-power load varies by exercise, athlete, method, external vs system power, body mass, and peak vs mean outcome
A universal "30% 1RM" rule
The acute peak-power load is the best chronic training load

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: profiling reliability and validity work is largely adult and vertical-jump-specific; the emerging individualization evidence is new, with varying profile methods, and requires downstream risk-of-bias review before organizational adoption.
modules.coach_judgment: whether to profile at all; how much weight a profile carries (CJ-03, CJ-04); the training load (CJ-01, CJ-02).

lessons.title: What the model does
lessons.content: Measured points, fitted relationship, derived parameters. Every step is an assumption doing work.

lessons.title: Reliability, stated in numbers
lessons.content: High linearity does not mean reliable slope; reported cross-method variation for slope is large enough that two methods can label the same athlete differently. That fact — not the label — is what coaches need.

lessons.title: Validity is method-dependent
lessons.content: Method selection materially changes interpretation, which means a profile without its method is uninterpretable.

lessons.title: External load-velocity is not muscle F-V
lessons.content: The two are routinely conflated; the conflation is what makes "deficit" language sound biological.

lessons.title: The load-power curve
lessons.content: Intermediate loads often maximize acute power, and the exact load moves with exercise, athlete, metric, and protocol. G3 publishes no percentage.

lessons.title: Acute versus chronic
lessons.content: §2.4's acute–chronic rule applied to loading: what produced the highest power once does not determine the training load for twelve weeks.

lessons.title: When to profile
lessons.content: An organizational question, answered by AS-105-11: does it change a decision here, at acceptable cost, with a method you can standardize?

modules.coaching_applications: In most G3 environments profiling is optional. Where it is used, the defensible form is: one standardized method, transparent protocol, results described rather than labeled, and any hypothesis corroborated against actual performance and observation before it changes a program.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Reading a profile as a diagnosis (D105-09, AS-105-08) · prescribing 30% 1RM (CA-04) · using an acute peak-power load as the chronic load (CA-05) · comparing profiles across methods or devices · treating "optimal profile" as a target · letting a profile replace observation.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M4-A — "Velocity deficient." An athlete labeled from a single profile. The learner examines reliability, assumptions, and corroboration, and states what the label may and may not license. Developed in full as Case 4 (§10.4).

knowledge_assessment.item: F0 and V0 are best described as…
Two methods produce different slope values for the same athlete. What follows?
The load producing highest acute power is best used for…
"The profile shows a force deficit, so we're doing a strength block." Identify the errors.
State the conditions under which G3 would use profiling at all.

applied_assessment.title: Profile interpretation
applied_assessment.description: Given a supplied profile with protocol details, the learner writes what it describes, what it cannot establish, one hypothesis it could support, the corroboration required, and the decision it would and would not change.
applied_assessment.standard: no diagnosis; method limits stated; no load percentage; corroboration specified.

modules.practical_sign_off_linkage: PS-1 — Power Evaluation & Method Selection. See §14.2. PS-1 gates M5.

modules.title: Ballistic Training & Explosive Intent
modules.framing_statement: Trying to move fast and moving fast are related, and they are not the same thing. Both matter, and the difference is coachable.
modules.purpose: To teach ballistic methods as a viable family with defined boundaries, and to establish intent as a real training variable without overclaiming what intent alone achieves.

learning_objectives.objective: Define ballistic exercise by continued acceleration or projection.
Select among loaded jumps, jump squats, bench throws, and ballistic push-ups by athlete and constraint.
Explain why ballistic intent is not the same as light load.
Apply maximal concentric intent appropriately across loads.
State what intent alone does and does not establish.
Select loading without a universal percentage.
Preserve output quality within a ballistic set.

evidence_classifications.statement: Ballistic, plyometric, and weightlifting methods are all viable power-training categories
Jump squat / loaded jump as a method
evidence_classifications.class: B — reasonable for trained adolescents and adults; youth use requires competence and supervision

evidence_classifications.statement: Bench throw as a method
evidence_classifications.class: B — most evidence from trained adult males; requires equipment and spotting

evidence_classifications.statement: Explosive push-up as a method
No single peak-power load is universally superior
Ballistic intent is not identical to using a light load
Maximal intended concentric acceleration is a relevant training principle
Intent alone guarantees identical adaptation across loads
"Explosive intent matters only with light loads"
"Power training must use light loads"

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: bench-throw and much ballistic evidence comes from resistance-trained adult males; youth application requires competence, supervision, and progression rather than scaled adult loading (Condition 2).
modules.coach_judgment: the load (CJ-01, CJ-02); which ballistic variants suit this athlete and facility.

lessons.title: What makes a movement ballistic
lessons.content: Continued acceleration through the movement or implement release, rather than deliberate end-range deceleration.

lessons.title: The family
lessons.content: Jumps, loaded jumps, jump squats, bench throws, ballistic push-ups, medicine-ball throws — with their equipment, spotting, and tolerance demands stated.

lessons.title: Intent versus load
lessons.content: A light non-ballistic lift may still require deceleration; a ballistic movement may permit fuller acceleration. Load and ballistic character are different variables.

lessons.title: Intent across loads
lessons.content: Maximal intended concentric acceleration is relevant even where external velocity is constrained by a heavy load — and it does not make heavy and light training equivalent.

lessons.title: Selecting the load
lessons.content: By intended adaptation, athlete competence, and preserved output. No percentage. Where a coach uses a descriptive load test, it describes that athlete in that exercise on that day.

lessons.title: Quality within the set
lessons.content: What output decline looks like, and the stop criteria the coach sets in advance (AS-105-04).

lessons.title: Benefit-to-cost
lessons.content: AS-105-03 applied: when a simpler ballistic option delivers the needed stimulus at lower equipment, learning, and supervision cost, it is the better selection.

modules.coaching_applications: For a G3 group with limited equipment, unloaded and lightly loaded jump variants plus medicine-ball throws cover most ballistic needs with low technical and equipment overhead — a defensible selection under AS-105-03, not a compromise.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Light-load-only power training (CA-03) · a universal 30% 1RM (CA-04) · intent claimed to matter only with light loads (CA-17) · using the acute peak-power load as the training load (CA-05) · sets long enough that the last reps train something else · loaded jumps prescribed to athletes without the competence to land them.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M5-A — 30% for everything. A coach prescribing 30% 1RM across all power exercises. The learner separates the useful idea from the unsupported rule and rewrites the prescription logic. Developed in full as Case 3 (§10.3).

knowledge_assessment.item: Ballistic exercise is defined by…
"Explosive intent only matters when the load is light."
Which factors govern ballistic load selection in G3?
"Research says 30% 1RM is optimal for power." Identify the errors.
State your stop criterion for a ballistic set and why.

applied_assessment.title: Ballistic prescription
applied_assessment.description: For one athlete: method, load basis, intent instruction, set structure, stop criteria, and the alternatives considered under AS-105-03.
applied_assessment.standard: no percentage asserted as a rule; intent and load distinguished; stop criteria observable; alternatives stated.

Prerequisite: PS-1 recorded (hard gate) and M4 at standard. Unlocks: M6.

modules.title: Plyometrics, Reactive Strength & Landing
modules.framing_statement: "Plyometrics" names a family whose members differ more than they resemble each other. Progress the demand, not the count.
modules.purpose: To teach plyometric training as a family of distinct demands, RSI as a task ratio rather than a diagnosis, and landing as a coached, progressed exposure with conservative safety language.

learning_objectives.objective: Describe the SSC without reducing it to stored elastic energy.
Distinguish plyometric tasks by landing, eccentric, contact-time, coordination, and tissue demand.
State what plyometric training is supported to improve.
Interpret RSI and RSI-modified as task-specific ratios.
Coach and progress landing and braking demand.
Progress plyometric demand rather than contact count.
Apply conservative causal language to landing and injury claims.

evidence_classifications.statement: Plyometric training is a family of rapid SSC tasks with substantially different demands under one label
Plyometric training improves jump and, in many populations, sprint and COD performance
Effects cannot be attributed exclusively to one mechanism such as tendon stiffness or RFD
Plyometric versus resistance training shows no consistent difference for jump outcomes; one review found plyometrics superior at 5 m and 20 m sprint with no difference in several other outcomes
"Stored elastic energy" as a complete explanation of SSC performance
evidence_classifications.class: F — neural activation, active muscle force, joint mechanics, pre-activation, and coordination also matter

evidence_classifications.statement: The ~250 ms fast/slow SSC boundary as a validated biological threshold
RSI is a standardized task-specific ratio
RSI alone completely measures reactive ability
Low RSI directly identifies a tendon-stiffness deficit
RSI/RSI-modified contributing to a broader standardized monitoring battery
Progressive, supervised landing exposure
Single-cue injury-prevention claims for landing
Universal contact-count classifications as evidence-based prescriptions
Twice-weekly training over ~8–10 weeks associated with more stable improvements in adolescent team-sport samples
evidence_classifications.class: B — sample-specific, not a universal prescription

evidence_classifications.statement: "Depth jumps are the best plyometric" / "more contacts = more power" / "every jump must be maximal"

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: much plyometric meta-analytic evidence is youth and team-sport specific with high heterogeneity; the dose finding above concerns adolescent team-sport samples and is not generalized.
modules.coach_judgment: the dose (CJ-08); whether and when depth jumps are used (CJ-09); progression rate.

lessons.title: The SSC, honestly
lessons.content: Eccentric, transition, concentric. Elastic behavior matters and does not explain performance alone. The ~250 ms convention is a convention.

lessons.title: The family, sorted by demand
lessons.content: Countermovement jumps, hops, bounds, drop and depth jumps, unilateral and bilateral, horizontal and vertical — sorted by landing force, eccentric demand, contact time, coordination, and tissue loading rather than by name.

lessons.title: What plyometrics are supported to improve
lessons.content: Jump outcomes robustly; sprint and COD in many populations; with heterogeneity stated and mechanism claims withheld.

lessons.title: RSI and RSI-modified
lessons.content: What the ratios are, what standardization they require, and what they cannot tell you (D105-12).

lessons.title: Landing as the trained quality
lessons.content: Braking and eccentric absorption; height, surface, direction, support, fatigue, and technique as the variables. Progressive supervised exposure is supported; single-cue prevention claims are not.

lessons.title: Progress demand, not contacts
lessons.content: AS-105-05: landing demand, velocity, amplitude, direction, unilateral demand, external load, complexity, exposure. No contact classification is published.

lessons.title: Safety language
lessons.content: The accurate sentence, rehearsed: exposure and progression are defensible; guarantees are not (§19, CJ-22).

modules.coaching_applications: In G3 Volleyball Development the binding issue is usually that practice already supplies enormous jump and landing volume. The competent plan counts it first (AS-105-15) and often reduces gym contacts while raising their quality — which is Case 5.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Counting contacts instead of progressing demand (CA-11) · treating depth jumps as universally best (CA-10) · every jump maximal (CA-12) · RSI read as reactive ability (CA-20) · low RSI read as a tendon diagnosis · plyometrics called inherently high risk (CA-08) · a landing cue promised to prevent ACL injury (CJ-22).

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M6-A — Below the team norm. An athlete whose RSI sits below the squad average. The learner states what that does and does not indicate and what they would do next. Developed in full as Case 8 (§10.8).

knowledge_assessment.item: Which demands differentiate plyometric tasks?
RSI is best described as…
The ~250 ms SSC boundary should be treated as…
"This landing cue prevents ACL injuries." Identify the error and rewrite the claim.
Name four ways to progress plyometric demand other than adding contacts.

applied_assessment.title: Plyometric progression
applied_assessment.description: A three-stage progression for a named athlete: task, landing demand, velocity and amplitude, direction, support, exposure, progression criterion, regression, and the parent- or athlete-facing safety sentence.
applied_assessment.standard: demand progressed rather than counted; criterion observable; no contact prescription; no injury guarantee.

modules.practical_sign_off_linkage: PS-2 (completed at M7). Observed elements from M6: the coach teaches and progresses a landing or plyometric task.

modules.title: Weightlifting Derivatives, Medicine Balls & Upper-Body Power
modules.framing_statement: The clean is a good tool with a large tuition fee. Whether an athlete should pay it is a coaching decision, not an identity.
modules.purpose: To evaluate weightlifting derivatives, medicine-ball work, and upper-body ballistics on benefit-to-cost, and to settle the "required versus dangerous" argument in both directions.

learning_objectives.objective: State what weightlifting training is supported to improve.
Weigh learning cost, equipment, mobility demand, opportunity cost, and coach competence.
Describe no-catch derivatives and their evidence status.
State why catching is not established as necessary.
Select medicine-ball tasks by movement, implement, and intended output.
Select upper-body power methods with their evidence limits stated.
Answer both the "required" and the "too dangerous" claims accurately.

evidence_classifications.statement: Weightlifting training is effective for strength, CMJ, squat jump, sprint, and COD-related outcomes
Weightlifting and plyometric training may yield similar improvements in speed, power, and strength outcomes
evidence_classifications.class: B — indicates utility, not unique necessity

evidence_classifications.statement: No method family is established as universally superior for every athlete and power outcome
Weightlifting movements carry high technical content; value depends on benefit exceeding learning cost, equipment, mobility demands, opportunity cost, and coach competence
No-catch derivatives may retain meaningful force-velocity exposure while reducing receiving-position constraints
evidence_classifications.basis: Evidence Pack §13; supporting record not itemized (§20.3b)

evidence_classifications.statement: "Every athlete must clean or snatch to develop power"
"Catching is necessary for power development"
"Olympic lifts are inherently too dangerous for athletes"
evidence_classifications.class: F/B boundary — risk depends on supervision, progression, and context

evidence_classifications.statement: Medicine-ball throws as a ballistic, projection-based option
A 12-week medicine-ball intervention in young female handball athletes produced greater throw-test gains than control
Universal medicine-ball load prescriptions and broad sport-transfer claims
Upper-body ballistic methods (bench throws, ballistic push-ups, upper-body plyometrics)
evidence_classifications.class: B/C — direct research more limited and exercise-specific

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: bench-throw evidence is largely resistance-trained men; the medicine-ball intervention evidence is young female handball athletes and sport/test specific. Neither generalizes automatically.
modules.coach_judgment: whether to teach weightlifting derivatives here (CJ-07); which variant; medicine-ball loading.

lessons.title: What weightlifting delivers
lessons.content: Effective across strength, jump, sprint, and COD-related outcomes — and comparable to plyometric training in several of them. Useful, not necessary.

lessons.title: The tuition fee
lessons.content: Technical content, coaching competence, equipment, mobility and receiving demands, and the opportunity cost of the time spent learning. AS-105-03 in its most consequential application.

lessons.title: No-catch derivatives
lessons.content: Pulls, high pulls, jump shrugs — plausibly retaining force-velocity exposure with fewer constraints, on limited direct comparative evidence. Claims of identical adaptation stay conditional.

lessons.title: Medicine balls
lessons.content: A genuine ballistic option for upper-body, rotational, and whole-body sequencing. Specify movement, implement, task, and intended output — not "core power."

lessons.title: Upper-body power
lessons.content: Bench throws, ballistic push-ups, upper-body plyometrics; thinner and more exercise-specific evidence than lower-body jump research, stated as such.

lessons.title: Both absolutes, answered
lessons.content: "Required" is Class F. "Too dangerous" sits on an F/B boundary where supervision, progression, and context decide. Coaches practise both answers.

lessons.title: Choosing for this athlete
lessons.content: A worked benefit-to-cost comparison, which is Case 6.

modules.coaching_applications: In a G3 scholastic environment with one coach and thirty athletes, the honest weightlifting answer is usually a derivative selected for coachability at that ratio — or a loaded-jump or medicine-ball alternative that reaches the intended stimulus without the tuition. Either is defensible; the reasoning is what is assessed.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Olympic lifts declared required or inherently dangerous (CA-06) · catching declared necessary (CA-07) · medicine-ball work described as generic "core power" · upper-body evidence generalized beyond its exercise · a method chosen because the coach enjoys teaching it · learning cost ignored in a 30-athlete room.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M7-A — Cleans or loaded jumps. A benefit-to-cost comparison for a specific athlete, facility, and coach. Developed in full as Case 6 (§10.6).

knowledge_assessment.item: The weightlifting evidence is best summarized as…

The evidence status of no-catch derivatives is…
"Athletes have to clean to be powerful." / "Cleans are too dangerous for high schoolers." Identify both errors.
Rewrite "medicine-ball core power work" in G3 terms.

applied_assessment.title: Method comparison
applied_assessment.description: For one athlete and objective, compare two method families across intended adaptation, learning cost, equipment, supervision, opportunity cost, and expected benefit; select and defend one; state what would change the selection.
applied_assessment.standard: no method declared required or forbidden; costs quantified in coaching terms; evidence limits stated.

modules.title: RFD, Impulse & Force-Time Interpretation
modules.framing_statement: Force-time data is the most seductive information in the field. It looks like an explanation and it is a description.
modules.purpose: To make coaches capable of interpreting force-time constructs accurately, and to establish the measurement-window and reliability limits that prevent RFD and derived metrics from becoming field diagnoses.

learning_objectives.objective: Define RFD and state its measurement-window sensitivity.
Distinguish early and late RFD determinants.
Distinguish impulse, peak force, and RFD, and state when each is task-relevant.
Explain why strength improvement and RFD change are not the same.
State the reliability limits of derived force-time metrics.
Explain why no single force-time variable is universally primary.
State what field inference from force-time data can and cannot support.

evidence_classifications.statement: Early RFD is strongly influenced by rapid voluntary activation and motor-unit discharge rate
Both explosive and heavy-resistance training can improve RFD in various populations
Valid and reliable RFD measurement is difficult
Early and late RFD windows have different determinants; later windows are more influenced by maximal force capacity
Strength improvement does not necessarily produce RFD improvement
evidence_classifications.class: B — a specific intervention and sample

evidence_classifications.statement: Impulse is the force-time integral and is directly relevant when momentum must change within a constrained time
Peak force may be insufficient when achieved too late for the task
Any one force-time variable is universally primary
Several derived force-plate metrics show weaker or protocol-sensitive reliability than basic outcomes
Routine individual RFD diagnosis in field settings

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: RFD methodology evidence is laboratory-oriented and adult; field applicability is explicitly limited by the source itself.
modules.coach_judgment: whether force-time measurement is worth running in a given environment (CJ-19).

lessons.title: RFD defined and bounded
lessons.content: The force-time slope, and the fact that the number depends heavily on the window and method chosen.

lessons.title: Early and late
lessons.content: Early windows are activation- and method-sensitive; later windows reflect maximal force capacity as time becomes available. Two different questions with one name.

lessons.title: Impulse as the task question
lessons.content: When momentum must change in limited time, impulse is usually the more task-informative construct — magnitude, direction, and available time together.

lessons.title: Peak force, late
lessons.content: Force achieved after the task is over is not useful force. This is why peak values alone mislead in time-constrained tasks.

lessons.title: Strength up, RFD flat
lessons.content: A documented outcome, and a permanent caution against assuming one adaptation implies the other.

lessons.title: Reliability of the derived
lessons.content: Basic outcomes are generally more reliable than several derived eccentric, stiffness, and RFD variables — which is the mechanical basis for D105-11.

lessons.title: What a coach may infer
lessons.content: Description, comparison against the athlete's own standardized baseline, and hypothesis generation. Not cause.

modules.coaching_applications: For G3 environments with force plates, this module produces the pre-specified metric set: a small number of reliable outcomes chosen before testing, with everything else left uncollected or explicitly exploratory.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Using RFD and power interchangeably · comparing RFD values across windows or methods · assuming a strength gain produced an RFD gain · reporting derived metrics with the same confidence as basic outcomes · force plates treated as explanations (CA-19) · building a program around a single force-time variable.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M8-A — The dashboard. A force-plate report listing twenty-two metrics for one athlete. The learner selects the small set that could change a decision, states what each is for, and says what they would stop collecting.

knowledge_assessment.item: Early RFD is most influenced by…
Which statements about impulse are correct?
Maximal force improved; RFD did not. What follows?
"The plate shows low RFD, so he needs plyometrics." Identify the errors.
State why the measurement window matters when comparing RFD values.

applied_assessment.title: Force-time interpretation
applied_assessment.description: Given a supplied force-time report with protocol, the learner writes what each retained metric describes, what it cannot establish, which metrics they would drop and why, and one hypothesis the data could support.
applied_assessment.standard: no causal claim; window and reliability limits stated; metric set reduced with reasoning; hypothesis provisional.

modules.practical_sign_off_linkage: Feeds PS-3 — the force-time interpretation (A8) is required evidence at PS-3 — and carries into PS-4.

modules.title: Complex/Contrast, PAPE, Cluster Sets & VBT
modules.framing_statement: Four popular methods sit in this module. All four have real uses. None of them has the evidence its marketing implies.
modules.purpose: To evaluate complex/contrast training, PAPE, cluster sets, and VBT accurately — separating acute from chronic evidence and measurement capability from programming superiority.

learning_objectives.objective: Distinguish PAP from PAPE.
State what acute PAPE evidence supports and what it does not.
State the chronic evidence status of complex and contrast training.
Describe cluster sets and their conditional use.
State what VBT provides and what it requires to be useful.
Explain why no velocity-loss threshold is published.
Apply the acute–chronic rule to any method claim.

evidence_classifications.statement: PAP and PAPE are distinct terms and should not be used interchangeably
Acute PAPE effects occur in some contexts and are small and variable
A 2025 meta-analysis of VBT conditioning activities reported enhancement with a response window in the analyzed studies and substantial context dependence
evidence_classifications.class: B/C — acute outcomes only; the window describes those studies

evidence_classifications.statement: Complex and contrast training can be useful chronically
evidence_classifications.class: C/B — superiority over simpler programming not consistently established

evidence_classifications.statement: "PAPE proves complex training is superior long term"
Cluster sets can preserve repetition quality; a 2024 complex-training study reported more favorable changes in certain outcomes with cluster incorporation
"Cluster sets are inherently superior for power"
VBT can provide feedback and monitor load-velocity, effort, and within-session velocity loss
VBT usefulness depends on device validity, exercise specificity, loading, familiarity, and whether the measure changes a decision
"VBT is required for power development"
A universal velocity-loss cutoff
evidence_classifications.class: Not verified for all exercises and athletes

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: PAPE, VBT, and cluster evidence is dominated by resistance-trained adults, frequently male, in laboratory or controlled settings.
modules.coach_judgment: whether to use any of these methods; any local velocity-loss convention (CJ-10); rest within contrast pairs (CJ-11).

lessons.title: PAP and PAPE are different words
lessons.content: Physiological potentiation versus a subsequent performance improvement reflecting potentiation-fatigue balance. Using them interchangeably is where the overclaim starts.

lessons.title: What acute evidence shows
lessons.content: Small, variable, context-dependent enhancement under selected protocols. Where the pack reports a response window from its analyzed studies, that window describes those studies — it is not a G3 prescription (CJ-05 reasoning).

lessons.title: The chronic question
lessons.content: Complex and contrast methods can be useful; consistent superiority over simpler programming is not established and depends on status, pairing design, recovery, and total training quality.

lessons.title: Cluster sets
lessons.content: A quality-preservation tool with conditional supporting evidence. Useful when preserving velocity or power is the operational goal; not inherently superior.

lessons.title: VBT, honestly
lessons.content: Real feedback and real monitoring value, dependent on device, exercise, loading, familiarity, and whether it changes a decision. Not required, not superior, not dismissible.

lessons.title: Why no threshold
lessons.content: No universal velocity-loss cutoff is verified across exercises and athletes. A coach may set a local convention; it is documented as a convention with a review date.

lessons.title: The rule, applied
lessons.content: Coaches practise sorting method claims into acute and chronic bins, which is the reasoning T-01 probes.

modules.coaching_applications: The most common defensible G3 use is contrast pairing in a session where the objective is quality, with the coach able to say the pairing is an organizational choice with conditional support — not a potentiation system.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: PAPE cited as proof of chronic superiority (CA-23) · cluster sets declared inherently superior (CA-24) · VBT declared required (CA-18) · an imported velocity-loss threshold · a study's response window quoted as a prescription · dismissing all four methods because they are over-marketed.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M9-A — The complex block. A coach proposing a full block built on PAPE reasoning. The learner separates acute from chronic and rewrites the rationale. Developed in full as Case 10 (§10.10).

knowledge_assessment.item: PAPE differs from PAP in that…
The chronic evidence for complex training is best summarized as…
Which conditions govern VBT usefulness?
"We use 20% velocity loss because the research supports it." Identify the errors.
State the acute–chronic rule in your own words with one example.

applied_assessment.title: Method claim audit
applied_assessment.description: Given four method claims drawn from real coaching material, the learner classifies each as acute or chronic, assigns an evidence class, states what it licenses, and rewrites any overclaim.
applied_assessment.standard: acute and chronic separated; no threshold imported; no superiority claim retained; corrections not inverted.

modules.practical_sign_off_linkage: Feeds PS-3 — the method claim audit (A9) is required evidence at PS-3 — and carries into PS-4.

Prerequisite: M8 at standard. Unlocks: M10. Gate: none.
