modules.title: Dosage, Rest, Exercise Order & Weekly Integration
modules.framing_statement: The athlete's jumps in practice count. Every honest power dose starts by subtracting.
modules.purpose: To teach dose, rest, and order as quality-preservation decisions, and to integrate power exposure with the total high-output load the athlete already carries.

learning_objectives.objective: Set dose by preserved quality rather than by volume.
Apply rest to preserve intended output.
Sequence power work relative to other qualities.
Explain the basis and limits of "power first" sequencing.
Count existing sprint, jump, COD, strength, practice, and competition exposure.
State why no universal weekly frequency or microcycle model is published.
Define stop and modify criteria in advance.

evidence_classifications.statement: No exact power-training dose is established across methods
evidence_classifications.class: B for quality-oriented dosing; D for exact field prescriptions

evidence_classifications.statement: Power work generally requires more recovery than hypertrophy-oriented training when preserving output is the priority
Exact rest requirements vary by task, load, athlete, and objective
Velocity or power drop-off can indicate changing session quality where valid measurement exists
A universal velocity-loss cutoff
Prioritizing high-quality power and speed tasks before substantial fatigue when maximal output is the objective
No universal weekly frequency, high/low organization, or microcycle model is established
evidence_classifications.class: D for exact templates; B for integrating with total high-intensity load

evidence_classifications.statement: Plyometric interventions commonly used 1–3 sessions weekly over 4–16 weeks with no clear dose-response evidence for exact optimal variables
evidence_classifications.class: B — describes the intervention literature, not a prescription

evidence_classifications.statement: "More contacts always produces more power"
"Fatigue makes power work more sport-specific"
evidence_classifications.class: F/B boundary — may train fatigue tolerance, not maximal power

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: dose literature is heterogeneous across ages, sports, and training status; the descriptive intervention ranges above are not prescriptions for any G3 athlete.
modules.coach_judgment: dose, rest, frequency, order, and organization (CJ-08, CJ-10 through CJ-14).

lessons.title: Dose by quality
lessons.content: The criterion is whether the athlete is still producing the intended output. Volume is an input, not a goal.

lessons.title: Rest for output
lessons.content: More recovery than hypertrophy work when output is the priority; exact intervals contextual. No number published.

lessons.title: Order
lessons.content: "Power first" is supported principally as a practical way to protect speed, technique, and high-intensity output from preceding fatigue — a B/D position, not a universal law, and contrast work shows preceding strength work is sometimes deliberate.

lessons.title: Counting what exists
lessons.content: Sprint, jump, COD, strength, practice, and competition exposure — counted before anything is added (AS-105-15). In jump-heavy sports this usually reduces gym volume.

lessons.title: Weekly organization
lessons.content: No universal frequency, high/low model, or microcycle template. The interaction with practice, competition, training age, total workload, and recovery determines the practical dose.

lessons.title: Stop and modify criteria
lessons.content: Written in advance: what output decline, technical change, or landing quality change ends the exposure.

lessons.title: The subtraction habit
lessons.content: Building a week by removing redundant high-output exposure before adding anything.

modules.coaching_applications: For a G3 in-season team, this module usually produces fewer, better exposures placed where output can be expressed, with practice jump volume counted and gym contacts reduced accordingly — which is exactly Case 5.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Adding power volume to a full week · counting contacts as the dose (CA-11) · cutting rest to increase difficulty · importing a velocity-loss threshold · treating "power first" as an inviolable rule · justifying fatigued power work as sport-specific (CA-26) · no stop criteria written in advance.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M10-A — The jump-heavy week. A volleyball athlete with high practice jump volume and a gym plyometric program written independently of it. Developed in full as Case 5 (§10.5).

knowledge_assessment.item: The G3 criterion for power-training dose is…
"Power first" sequencing is best described as…
Which exposures must be counted under AS-105-15?
"Three sessions a week, 120 contacts each, that's the standard." Identify the errors.
State your stop criterion for a plyometric exposure and how you would observe it.

applied_assessment.title: Weekly integration
applied_assessment.description: For one real group: all existing high-output exposure counted, the power exposure placed and dosed, rest and order justified, stop criteria stated, and the Coach Judgment elements labeled.
applied_assessment.standard: existing load counted; no universal dose, frequency, or contact figure; criteria observable; week deliverable as written.

Prerequisite: M9 at standard. Unlocks: M11. Gate: none.

modules.title: Periodization, Maintenance, Youth & Female Athletes
modules.framing_statement: Two questions this module refuses to answer with a number: how much power work maintains power in-season, and what a female athlete needs that a male athlete does not.
modules.purpose: To organize power development over time without adopting a validated-sounding model, and to establish the youth and female-athlete positions this course carries.

learning_objectives.objective: Describe concurrent and mixed-method routes to strength and power adaptation.
Reject mandatory strength-then-power sequencing.
Describe named periodization systems as influential frameworks.
Prescribe in-season maintenance as a defended reduction with a verification plan.
State the unresolved status of exact maintenance and minimum-effective doses.
Apply youth progression by competence and exposure.
State the female-athlete evidence position and what it does and does not license.

evidence_classifications.statement: Multiple routes to strength and power adaptation are supported, including concurrent and mixed-method approaches
Mandatory strength-then-power sequencing
Phase potentiation, blocks, French contrast, triphasic and similar systems
evidence_classifications.class: E — influential applied frameworks, not universally validated templates

evidence_classifications.statement: Maintaining important neuromuscular exposures in-season with reduced volume and retained intensity/quality
Exact universal in-season maintenance and minimum-effective doses
Youth resistance and plyometric training can improve strength, jump, sprint, and other fitness outcomes when supervised and progressed
Age-based prohibitions and arbitrary strength thresholds as universal gates
Low injury rates in properly prescribed youth resistance training and weightlifting under supervision
Progression considering training age, coordination, maturity, exposure, and supervision
Youth evidence validating adult loading, volume, or testing prescriptions for middle-school athletes
Female athletes improve strength, jump, sprint, and COD outcomes through resistance and plyometric training
Fundamentally different power-training principles for female athletes
Broad cycle-based power prescriptions

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: many power-method studies are male-dominant; medicine-ball evidence includes young female handball samples but is sport-specific; youth evidence supports supervised progressive training without establishing adult prescriptions.
modules.coach_judgment: the organization (CJ-14); the in-season dose (CJ-15, CJ-16); individual modification for any athlete (CJ-21).

lessons.title: Multiple routes
lessons.content: Concurrent and mixed approaches are supported; no sequence is mandated. This closes the loop opened by D105-04.

lessons.title: Systems as frameworks
lessons.content: Phase potentiation, blocks, French contrast, triphasic, and similar systems taught as Class E — influential, organizing, not validated templates (§17.4).

lessons.title: In-season maintenance
lessons.content: Retain quality exposure at reduced volume where recovery permits. The exact dose is Unknown, and G3 publishes none — the form is a defended reduction with a verification plan, inherited from G3 104 M9.

lessons.title: Youth: what is supported
lessons.content: Supervised, progressed resistance and plyometric training improves outcomes; low injury rates in properly prescribed settings; no age gate; no strength-ratio gate.

lessons.title: Youth: what is not licensed
lessons.content: Adult loading, volume, and testing prescriptions do not transfer to middle-school athletes because a youth study showed a method is safe. Both halves are stated together.

lessons.title: Female athletes
lessons.content: Same foundational principles; individual sport demands, maturation, history, and recovery matter; cycle evidence is not converted into deterministic prescriptions; underrepresentation is disclosed at the point of the claim (§18.2).

lessons.title: Writing the block
lessons.content: Assembling M10's integration and this module's constraints into a real training period for a real athlete.

modules.coaching_applications: In G3 Youth S&C the module usually produces simpler exposures with real progression criteria and documented supervision; in-season it usually produces a smaller, protected, quality-first exposure with an explicit statement that maintenance — not development — is the objective.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: Strength-then-power sequencing (CA-16) · a named system presented as validated · publishing an in-season maintenance dose · age gates or strength gates for youth (CA-09, CA-02) · transferring adult prescriptions to middle-school athletes on the strength of a youth safety finding · building phase-based programming from cycle evidence (CJ-21).

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M11-A — The new twelve-year-old. A middle-school athlete new to power training, with a parent asking when "real" training starts. Developed in full as Case 1 (§10.1).

knowledge_assessment.item: The evidence on strength-then-power sequencing is…
Which factors govern youth power progression?
The evidence status of exact in-season power maintenance dose is…
"She's 12 — power training starts at 16." Identify the error.
State G3's female-athlete position and what it does not license.

applied_assessment.title: Contextual block
applied_assessment.description: A 6–10 week block for a named athlete: organization with its rationale labeled as judgment, maintenance handled as a defended reduction where relevant, youth or female considerations addressed with disclosure, and review points defined.
applied_assessment.standard: no model asserted as validated; no maintenance dose published; no gates; disclosures present.

modules.title: Testing, Force Plates, Readiness & Integrated G3 Decision-Making
modules.gating_summary: requires PS-3 · Sign-off: PS-4, then T-01
modules.framing_statement: The dashboard will offer you a diagnosis. The last thing this course does is teach you to decline it.
modules.purpose: To select and interpret power tests, govern technology use, refuse readiness and asymmetry thresholds, and run the full G3 decision model on a power case.

learning_objectives.objective: Select a test matching the construct being evaluated.
State what CMJ, squat jump, drop jump/RSI, broad jump, loaded jump, medicine-ball throw, and VBT velocity each measure.
Apply standardization: protocol, equipment, warm-up, instructions, calculation, baseline.
State the reliability limits of derived force-plate metrics.
Treat power equations as estimates.
Interpret change against baseline, typical error, and context.
Refuse universal readiness and asymmetry thresholds without substituting new ones.
Run the G3 decision model on a power case and defend it.

evidence_classifications.statement: CMJ height is a standardized vertical-jump outcome, not a complete power, RFD, or readiness diagnosis
Drop jump / RSI is a task-specific flight-to-contact ratio, not complete reactive ability, stiffness, or injury risk
Broad jump is a horizontal jump outcome, not a sprint-acceleration mechanism diagnosis
Loaded-jump results do not create universal F-V diagnoses
Medicine-ball throws are task-specific projection outcomes
VBT velocity is exercise-, load-, and device-specific
Force plates can measure force-time data and derive outcomes; reliability is metric-specific, with basic outcomes generally more reliable than several derived variables
Peak-power equations are estimates that may not match device-derived values or retain validity across body sizes, protocols, and populations
evidence_classifications.class: A/B for standardized jump height as an outcome; C/F for unqualified estimated-power claims

evidence_classifications.statement: Smartphone-based CMJ tools can show acceptable validity for selected metrics in specific implementations; validation is not automatically transferable
CMJ and related measures are useful within-person monitoring tools with standardized protocol, baseline, typical error, and decision context
Automated readiness determination from CMJ height, RSI-modified, or any single force-plate metric
No universal 10% or 15% asymmetry cutoff is established as automatically performance-limiting, injury-predictive, or corrective
evidence_classifications.class: F for universal cutoff interpretation; B/C for monitoring repeated task-specific asymmetry when reliable

modules.population_transfer_disclosure: CMJ metric and reliability work is device- and protocol-dependent, largely adult; app validation is implementation-specific.
modules.coach_judgment: which tests are feasible and decision-relevant in a given facility (CJ-19); how to interpret a measured asymmetry (CJ-20) or a readiness signal (CJ-18).

lessons.title: Construct first
lessons.content: Decide the construct, then the test. Reversing that order is how a jump becomes a readiness score.

lessons.title: What each test measures
lessons.content: The seven-row table in §15.2, taught as the operating reference.

lessons.title: Standardization
lessons.content: Protocol, equipment, warm-up, instructions, calculation method, and baseline — recorded at time of testing (AS-105-09, inherited G3 102 AS-06).

lessons.title: Reliability of the derived
lessons.content: Basic outcomes over dashboard breadth (D105-11), with the pre-specified metric set from M8.

lessons.title: Estimates are estimates
lessons.content: Power equations, flight-time methods, contact mats, cameras, and plates each carry assumptions; cross-system comparison is not interpretation.

lessons.title: Interpreting change
lessons.content: Baseline, typical error, context, and other athlete information — never one number (AS-105-12). This is Case 7.

lessons.title: Refusing the thresholds
lessons.content: No readiness threshold and no asymmetry cutoff, and no replacement number (AS-105-13). This is Case 9.

lessons.title: The integrated case
lessons.content: The full G3 102 model run on a power decision, producing the one-page plan the coach defends.

modules.coaching_applications: The artifact is a G3 power testing report another coach can read: what was measured, in what task, under what protocol, against what baseline, what it does and does not establish, and what decision it changed.

common_errors_claim_audit.text: CMJ height read as readiness (CA-22) · RSI read as reactive ability (CA-20) · force plates read as explanations (CA-19) · asymmetry read as a problem (CA-21) · estimated power compared across systems · a metric set chosen after the data arrived · running the decision model without naming the output requirement.

modules.case_scenario: Scenario M12-A — Full integration. A complete athlete file including a testing report with at least one unsupported inference. The learner runs the model, rewrites the report, and defends the plan. Cases 7, 8, or 9 may be substituted at the assessor's discretion.

cases.title: Middle-School Athlete New to Power Training
cases.situation: Ana, 12, joins a G3 Youth group of 18 with one coach, two 50-minute sessions weekly. No structured training history. Coordinated for her age, attentive, no injury history. She lands noisily and asymmetrically from a two-foot jump and has never been coached to land. Her father asks when she can start "real explosive training," and mentions a coach who told him power work should wait until 16 and until she can squat 1.5× bodyweight.
cases.decision_required: What does Ana's power exposure consist of, how does it progress, and what do you tell her father?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who introduces light external load once landing is competent passes with a stated criterion. A coach who stays unloaded for the block and says why also passes.
cases.failure_modes: Accepting either gate · substituting a different threshold · "explosiveness" language with a 12-year-old · adult contact counts or loading applied to youth · complexity beyond the supervision ratio · promising injury prevention · leaving landing uncoached because it looks like nothing.

cases.title: Strong High-School Athlete With Poor Acceleration
cases.situation: Marcus, 17, three years of well-coached strength training. Trap-bar deadlift and squat among the strongest in the program absolutely and relative to body mass. CMJ above team average. First-step and 10 m acceleration among the poorest in the squad, consistently, across two testing occasions on the same surface with the same timing method. Video shows a tall first step, late shin angle, and a hesitant initiation under reactive conditions. Sport practice is dense; there has been no dedicated sprint-technical exposure.
cases.decision_required: What is the limitation hypothesis, and what does the block contain?
cases.defensible_variation: A coach who prioritizes reactive and initiation work, or one who prioritizes sprint-technical exposure, both pass with the hypothesis and falsifier stated. Adding a strength block fails absent a force-capacity argument the data does not support.
cases.failure_modes: "He needs more power" as the plan · a jump metric used to diagnose acceleration · an F-V label applied without a profile, or with one · vector-matching justification · ignoring the absence of sprint exposure · a hypothesis with no falsifier.

cases.title: Coach Prescribing 30% 1RM for Every Power Exercise
cases.situation: A G3 coach has standardized every power exercise at 30% 1RM — jump squats, bench throws, and pulls — citing "the optimal power load." Athletes range from a 14-year-old novice to a fourth-year collegiate athlete. The coach also cites an in-house testing day where several athletes produced their highest measured power near that load in the jump squat.
cases.decision_required: What is right about this, what is wrong, and what replaces it?
cases.defensible_variation: Retaining a loading range as a starting point for a specific exercise and athlete, labeled as a working convention, passes. Retaining any figure as "the optimal power load" fails.
cases.failure_modes: Replacing 30% with another number · keeping the rule for one exercise "because it was measured" · dismissing the coach's testing entirely · treating the acute result as chronic evidence · applying a 1RM-percentage scheme to a novice youth athlete without comment.

cases.title: Athlete Labeled "Velocity Deficient" From One F-V Profile
cases.situation: Sofia, 19, collegiate athlete. A single vertical-jump force-velocity profile, collected once on a portable system by a visiting practitioner using a method the G3 staff cannot fully reconstruct, returns a label: "velocity deficient, prioritize velocity-oriented training." Her sprint and jump performance are unremarkable but not poor. No sprint testing, no technical observation, and no training history were included. The sport coach has seen the label and is asking about a velocity block.
cases.defensible_variation: Discarding the profile and evaluating from scratch passes. Retaining it as one input, corroborated, passes. Building the velocity block fails.
cases.failure_modes: Accepting the label · rejecting profiling entirely in reaction · comparing this profile to one collected by another method · recording "velocity deficient" as an athlete attribute · using "optimal profile" as the target (CJ-03) · letting the sport coach's expectation set the program.

cases.title: Volleyball Athlete With High Jump Volume
cases.situation: A G3 Volleyball Development athlete, 16, mid-season. Five practices weekly with high jump volume, a Saturday tournament format with up to five matches, and two G3 slots. The current gym program includes a plyometric block written at the start of the season and unchanged since — three sessions weekly with a fixed contact count. The athlete reports persistent lower-leg soreness and her landing quality visibly degrades late in practice.
cases.defensible_variation: Any reduction justified by the counted exposure passes, including removing gym plyometrics entirely for a period while retaining landing quality work. Keeping the fixed contact count fails.
cases.failure_modes: Adding volume to a full week · retaining a fixed contact prescription · reading soreness as effectiveness · declaring plyometrics unsafe · ignoring the landing-quality observation · promising the change prevents injury.

cases.title: Olympic Lifts vs Loaded Jumps
cases.situation: A G3 scholastic program, one coach, 28 athletes, two 45-minute slots, limited platforms and bumper plates, mixed training ages from novice to third-year. The head coach — who is competent in weightlifting and enjoys teaching it — proposes teaching the power clean to the whole squad as the primary power method. A staff member argues Olympic lifts are too dangerous for high schoolers and should be replaced with loaded jumps.
cases.decision_required: Which method, and how do you answer both arguments?
cases.failure_modes: Method chosen by coach preference or by fear · either absolute retained · learning cost ignored · no-catch equivalence overclaimed · the constraint of 28:1 in 45 minutes left out of the reasoning entirely.

cases.title: CMJ Drops 4% Before Practice
cases.situation: A morning CMJ screen returns a 4% drop from the athlete's recorded value for one athlete, taken on a contact mat, one trial, after a shortened warm-up because the group was late. The athlete reports normal sleep and no pain, moved well in the warm-up, and has a competition in four days. The platform's dashboard flags the athlete amber and suggests a reduced session. The sport coach has seen the flag.
cases.decision_required: Is this athlete ready to train?
cases.defensible_variation: Modest in-session adjustment based on observation passes. Reducing the session on the flag alone fails, as does ignoring the athlete entirely.
cases.failure_modes: Automatic "not ready" · deferring to the dashboard · treating one trial as a baseline · comparing across protocols · substituting a different percentage threshold · dismissing monitoring altogether.

cases.title: RSI Below Team Norm
cases.situation: A drop-jump screen returns an RSI below the team average for one athlete. A staff member proposes a "tendon stiffness block" on the basis that low RSI indicates a reactive or stiffness deficit. The athlete performs well in sport, has no symptoms, and — on video — visibly uses a deeper, longer contact strategy than her teammates, from a drop height she has never trained.
cases.decision_required: What does the RSI value indicate?
cases.defensible_variation: Adding progressive reactive exposure because her sport demands it passes. Coaching contact strategy and re-measuring passes. A stiffness block justified by the RSI value fails.
cases.failure_modes: Diagnosing tendon stiffness (CA-20) · treating the team mean as a standard · ignoring the strategy visible on video · running a corrective block that displaces the athlete's actual priority · abandoning RSI as useless in reaction.

cases.title: 12% Interlimb Asymmetry
cases.situation: A single-leg jump screen returns a 12% interlimb difference, tested once, on a portable system, at the end of a training week. No pain, no injury history on either side, normal practice and competition performance, unremarkable bilateral results. A staff member cites a 10% threshold and proposes a corrective block.
cases.defensible_variation: Monitoring repeated task-specific asymmetry where the measure is reliable passes. Acting on this single value fails, as does adopting any threshold.
cases.failure_modes: Acting on one measurement · adopting the 10% threshold · substituting another number · declaring an injury risk · dismissing asymmetry monitoring entirely · displacing the athlete's actual training priority with a corrective block.

cases.title: Complex Training and PAPE
cases.situation: A coach proposes rebuilding the squad's power block around complex training, arguing that PAPE research demonstrates superiority over separate strength and power work. The proposal cites an acute meta-analysis reporting performance enhancement after conditioning activities, and specifies a fixed rest window taken from that analysis. The squad is scholastic, mixed training age, two slots weekly.
cases.decision_required: What is defensible in this proposal, and what is the rewrite?
cases.defensible_variation: Using complex pairing passes. Not using it passes. Retaining the superiority claim in any hedged form fails.
cases.failure_modes: Acute evidence cited as chronic proof (CA-23) · an imported rest window presented as a prescription · population transfer ignored · cluster sets or contrast pairing declared inherently superior (CA-24) · abandoning the structure entirely in reaction to the overclaim.
